title: Piano Quintet No. 2 in A major
hook: Five players, two Slavic dances and a lament that keeps breaking into joy.

painting.title: Company in the Country
painting.pairingNote: A Czech painter’s summer outing by a stream, friends lounging and girls wading in the water, two years after Dvořák wrote this sunny quintet in the country at Vysoká.

facts: Dvořák wrote the quintet between 18 August and 3 October 1887, much of it at Vysoká, his summer house in the Bohemian countryside. He had just been revising his first piano quintet, written fifteen years earlier in the same key; instead of patching up the old piece, he wrote a new one that shares nothing with it but the key and the five instruments.

It was first played in Prague on 6 January 1888, at the Rudolfinum. A month later Tchaikovsky visited Prague and heard it at a soirée in his honour. He wrote in his diary that he “very much liked his quintet”.

Two of the four movements are named after Slavic folk forms: a [[dumka|dumka]], a lament that swings between brooding and high spirits, and a [[furiant|furiant]], a fiery Czech dance. Dvořák wrote his own tunes in folk style; he quotes no real folk song.
The piano is not a soloist with a string quartet behind it. The five players share the themes, and the cello and viola get some of the best tunes.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a warm song that keeps flaring up (I), a lament with sudden bursts of joy (II), a whirling dance with a dreamy centre (III), a high-spirited romp with a fugue and a hushed chorale before the final dash (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro ma non tanto
movements.summary: The cello sings a long, warm melody over a gentle, rippling piano. Within half a minute the mood darkens: the same tune bursts out loud in the minor. The whole movement plays with this double face of its themes, sunny and stormy. It is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], with a second theme for the viola.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, cello
mainIdeas.description: a broad, singing melody in A major over even, rocking piano chords.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, viola
mainIdeas.description: a busier, more restless melody, in the minor.

stops.hear: The piano ripples softly; the cello enters with a long, warm melody
Suddenly loud and dark: all five players hurl the tune out in the minor
The first violin takes the melody up high, and the music brightens again
stops.happening: The theme passed around the group

stops.hear: The viola starts a new, more restless tune; the piano answers
Fragments of both themes in new keys, passed between piano and strings
The cello’s melody returns, slightly changed
The music speeds up and gathers all five players

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Loud, bright chords and a quick, exultant ending

notice: Follow the cello’s opening melody through the movement. It turns up in the violin, in the piano, in the minor, at full volume, and almost never the same way twice.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Curzon recorded this quintet with the Vienna Philharmonic Quartet, led by the orchestra’s concertmaster Willi Boskovsky, in the Sofiensaal in Vienna in October 1962; John Culshaw produced it. They do not repeat the first part of the first movement, which is why it lasts about ten minutes; performances that take the repeat last around thirteen. On the Spotify album the quintet is tracks 5–8, after Dvořák’s String Quartet, Op. 51, played by the Boskovsky Quartet.

movements.heading: Dumka. Andante con moto
movements.summary: A dumka is a Slavic lament, and Dvořák makes it a pattern of sudden contrasts. A sad, swaying melody in F-sharp minor returns again and again, each time richer; between its returns come a brighter, gentler section and, in the middle, a fast, wild dance built from the lament itself. The scheme is A–B–A–C–A–B–A, a kind of [[rondo|rondo]].

mainIdeas.name: The lament
mainIdeas.description: a slow, melancholy tune on the piano, over a gently rocking accompaniment, then taken up by the viola.

mainIdeas.name: The bright episode
mainIdeas.description: a softer, more hopeful tune in D major for the violins.

mainIdeas.name: The fast episode
mainIdeas.description: the lament’s melody turned into a quick, stamping dance.

stops.hear: The piano plays a sad, swaying melody; the viola takes it up, darker still
stops.happening: The dumka theme (A), in F-sharp minor

stops.hear: The mood lifts: the violins sing a gentler, more hopeful tune
stops.happening: The bright episode (B), in D major

stops.hear: The lament returns, with a fuller accompaniment
Suddenly fast and loud: the lament’s tune rushes by as a whirling dance
The slow lament comes back, as if nothing had happened
The gentle, hopeful tune again

stops.label: Last 2 minutes
stops.hear: The lament one last time, then a quiet close

notice: Listen for the moment around the middle when the slow lament suddenly turns into a fast dance. The tune is the same; only the speed and the mood have changed.
Each time the lament returns, notice what has been added around it: a new counter-melody, a richer piano part, a different instrument on the tune.

movements.heading: Scherzo (Furiant). Molto vivace
movements.summary: A furiant is a fast Czech folk dance, and here it whirls. The first violin leads with a quick, swirling tune while the viola and cello pluck the beat beneath. In the middle a slower, dreamy section uses the same material more quietly, with piano and violin trading the melody. Then the dance returns and ends abruptly.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a fast, spinning tune in the first violin over plucked strings.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: a slower, misty version of the dance, piano and violin taking turns.

stops.hear: A fast, whirling tune in the first violin; viola and cello pluck underneath
stops.happening: The furiant, in A major. The plucking is [[pizzicato|pizzicato]]

stops.hear: The piano joins in and the dance gathers force
Everything calms and slows; piano and violin pass a soft, dreamy melody between them
The whirling dance comes back

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A sudden burst and a sharp, emphatic ending
stops.happening: The movement ends without slowing down

notice: Dvořák’s furiant does not use the dance’s trademark stumble between two and three beats; it keeps a steady, driving three. What makes it a furiant is its fire.

movements.heading: Finale. Allegro
movements.summary: A cheerful, bustling finale, light on its feet, with three themes. In the middle the second violin starts a little [[fugue|fugue]] on the main tune and the others join one by one. Near the end everything stops for a hushed, hymn-like passage; then the music gathers speed and the quintet rushes to a brilliant finish.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a quick, skipping tune, bright and good-humoured.

mainIdeas.name: The chorale
mainIdeas.description: the main tune slowed right down and played very softly, like a hymn.

stops.hear: A quick, skipping tune, bright and good-humoured
A smoother, singing melody
The second violin starts the main tune alone; the others join in one after another
The skipping opening tune is back
Everything goes quiet; the main tune is played slowly and softly, like a hymn

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The music speeds up and dashes to a loud, brilliant close

notice: Just before the end, listen for the very quiet, slow passage. It is the finale’s own tune, stretched out into a hymn, a moment of stillness before the last dash.

threads.title: Folk spirit without folk songs
threads.body: The dumka and the furiant are Slavic forms, but every tune is Dvořák’s own. The national colour comes from rhythms, moods and sudden contrasts, not quotations.

threads.title: Light and shade
threads.body: The first movement’s sunny tune that turns stormy, the dumka’s flips from lament to dance: the quintet keeps switching between brooding and joy, and joy wins.

threads.title: Five equals
threads.body: The cello opens the work, the viola introduces the second theme, the second violin starts the fugue. The piano is the glue, not the star.
